entries.meaning: An area of land with its buildings, used for growing crops or raising animals. ---
examples: My grandparents ran a small dairy farm up north.
Most of the farms around here grow corn and soybeans.
We buy our eggs straight from the farm.

entries.meaning: The work or business of running a farm. ---
examples: Farming is harder work than most people imagine.
He gave up farming after three bad years in a row.
Organic farming has grown fast in this part of the state.

entries.meaning: The science and practice of growing crops and raising animals for food. ---
examples: Agriculture still employs a lot of people out here.
She studied agriculture at a state university.
The new bill sets water rules for agriculture and industry alike.

entries.meaning: The practice of growing different crops in the same field in successive years to keep the soil healthy. ---
examples: Crop rotation cuts down on pests without any spraying.
He uses a four-year crop rotation on the back fields.
Without crop rotation, the soil wears out fast.

entries.meaning: A machine that cuts and gathers a ripe crop. ---
examples: The harvester broke down in the middle of the field.
Two harvesters worked the wheat until well after dark.
He rents a harvester instead of buying one.

entries.meaning: A large machine that cuts grain and separates the seed from the stalks in one pass. ---
examples: A combine was crawling along the far edge of the field.
The neighbors share a combine to save money.
Modern combines cost more than a house.
entries.contrast: The machine is stressed on the first syllable, KAHM-byne; the verb to combine is stressed on the second, kuhm-BYNE.

entries.meaning: A farm tool with heavy blades, pulled through soil to turn it over before planting. ---
examples: The plow is hitched to the back of the tractor.
He keeps two old plows rusting behind the barn.
A single plow used to take a whole team of horses.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it plow; the British spell the same word plough. Both rhyme with cow.

entries.meaning: The supplying of water to farmland through ditches, pipes, or sprinklers. ---
examples: Without irrigation, nothing would grow in that valley.
The farm switched to drip irrigation to save water.
Irrigation accounts for most of the county's water use.

entries.meaning: The amount of a crop that a piece of land produces. ---
examples: This year's corn yield was the best in a decade.
Wet weather cut yields by almost a third.
The new seed promises a higher yield per acre.

entries.meaning: Land that is used or suitable for farming. ---
examples: Housing developments keep eating up good farmland.
They own eighty acres of prime farmland.
The road runs through flat farmland for thirty miles.

entries.meaning: Farmland that is plowed and planted with crops rather than left for grazing. ---
examples: Half the county's cropland is planted in soybeans.
They converted some pasture into cropland.
Flooding ruined thousands of acres of cropland.

entries.meaning: Open, unplanted land where livestock are left to graze. ---
examples: The ranch leases federal rangeland for its cattle.
Dry summers have thinned the grass on the rangeland.
Most of the state's rangeland lies east of the mountains.

entries.meaning: A large farm in the western United States where cattle, sheep, or horses are raised. ---
examples: They run a cattle ranch out west.
Both ranches were sold to the same buyer.
We spent a week on a working ranch last summer.

entries.meaning: A large estate where a single crop such as cotton, sugar, or coffee is grown. ---
examples: The coffee comes from a small plantation in the hills.
Rubber plantations covered most of the island.
He inherited a run-down plantation from an uncle.

entries.meaning: A house and the farmland around it, worked by one family. ---
examples: The old homestead has been in the family five generations.
Settlers claimed homesteads along the river.
Nothing is left of the homestead but a stone chimney.

entries.meaning: A farmhouse together with the barns and sheds that stand around it. ---
examples: A row of maples shelters the farmstead from the wind.
Several abandoned farmsteads dot the back roads.
The whole farmstead needs a new roof.

entries.meaning: The main house on a farm, where the farmer lives. ---
examples: Supper is served in the farmhouse at six sharp.
They restored a hundred-year-old farmhouse.
Most of the farmhouses out here have wide front porches.

entries.meaning: The open, fenced area next to a barn where farm animals are kept. ---
examples: Chickens scratched around the muddy barnyard.
He hosed down the barnyard after the rain.
The dog sleeps by the gate at the edge of the barnyard.

entries.meaning: A field of grass that is grown and cut for hay. ---
examples: The hayfield was cut twice last summer.
Deer bed down in the hayfields at dusk.
He drove the mower slowly across the hayfield.

entries.meaning: A field planted with corn. ---
examples: The kids got lost in the cornfield for an hour.
Cornfields stretch to the horizon on both sides.
A dirt road cuts straight through the cornfield.

entries.meaning: A small fenced field, usually where horses are turned out. ---
examples: Two mares were grazing in the paddock.
He turns the colts out into the paddock every morning.
The paddocks nearest the barn have the best grass.

entries.meaning: A fenced pen for holding cattle or horses. ---
examples: They drove the steers into the corral at sundown.
One of the corral gates was hanging off its hinge.
The horses circled the corral twice before settling.
entries.contrast: Stressed on the second syllable, kuh-RAL — don't confuse it with coral, KOR-uhl, the reef.

entries.meaning: A fenced area where cattle are kept and fattened on grain before slaughter. ---
examples: The calves go to a feedlot at about a year old.
You can smell the feedlot from the highway.
Large feedlots handle tens of thousands of cattle.

entries.meaning: A set of pens where livestock are held before being sold or shipped. ---
examples: The cattle spent a night in the stockyard.
The old stockyards by the rail line are gone now.
Buyers walk the stockyard early on sale day.

entries.meaning: A large, continuous piece of land. ---
examples: He bought a forty-acre tract next to the creek.
Several tracts of farmland came up for auction.
The state protected a tract of prairie from development.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like tracked, the past tense of track.

entries.meaning: The dark upper layer of soil, where most plant roots grow. ---
examples: Heavy rain washed the topsoil off the slope.
We hauled in a truckload of topsoil for the garden.
There's barely six inches of topsoil on that hillside.

entries.meaning: The harder, paler layer of soil lying under the topsoil. ---
examples: The plow bit down into heavy subsoil.
Water drains slowly through this subsoil.
Roots reach the subsoil only in a dry year.

entries.meaning: Rich, crumbly soil that is a good mix of sand, silt, and clay. ---
examples: Tomatoes do best in deep, well-drained loam.
The bottomland is dark loam a foot thick.
He crumbled a handful of loam between his fingers.

entries.meaning: The dark, rotted plant matter in soil that makes it fertile. ---
examples: Years of manure built up the humus in that field.
Forest soil is full of humus.
Compost adds humus to worn-out ground.
entries.contrast: HYOO-muhs, the soil — not hummus, HUM-uhs, the chickpea dip.

entries.meaning: Fine soil carried by moving water and left behind when it slows. ---
examples: The flood left three inches of silt on the field.
Silt has nearly filled the irrigation pond.
River bottoms here are rich with silt.

entries.meaning: The gradual wearing away of soil by wind or water. ---
examples: Cover crops slow erosion over the winter.
You can see erosion along every ditch bank.
Plowing up and down the slope makes erosion worse.
entries.contrast: The s is pronounced like the s in measure: ih-ROH-zhuhn.

entries.meaning: The ability of soil to grow healthy crops. ---
examples: Manure restored some of the field's fertility.
Constant corn drains the soil's fertility.
They test each field for fertility every spring.

entries.meaning: A substance that a plant or animal needs in order to grow. ---
examples: Heavy rain washes nutrients out of the topsoil.
The lab report shows which nutrient the field is short of.
Beans put a key nutrient back into the ground.
entries.contrast: Americans say NOO-tree-uhnt; the British say NYOO-tree-uhnt.

entries.meaning: A chemical containing phosphorus, spread on fields to help plants grow. ---
examples: They spread phosphate on the corn ground in the fall.
Phosphates running off farms end up in the lake.
The soil test called for more phosphate.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: Both ph spellings are said as f: FAHS-fayt.

entries.meaning: A potassium compound used as fertilizer. ---
examples: The blend is mostly nitrogen with some potash.
Potash prices doubled in two years.
Alfalfa takes a lot of potash out of the soil.

entries.meaning: A chemical used to kill weeds. ---
examples: He sprayed herbicide along the fence line.
Some weeds now shrug off the common herbicides.
The label says to keep the herbicide off nearby crops.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: Most Americans drop the h: UR-buh-syde, like herb. The British sound it: HUR-bih-syde.

entries.meaning: A chemical used to kill or stop the fungus that causes plant disease. ---
examples: A single fungicide spray saved the apple crop.
Wet springs mean more fungicides on the vines.
He mixed the fungicide according to the label.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: The g is soft, like the g in gem: FUN-juh-syde.

entries.meaning: The work of turning over soil with a plow. ---
examples: Plowing starts as soon as the ground dries out.
He finished the plowing by the end of the week.
Deep plowing buries last year's stubble.

entries.meaning: The work of putting seeds or young plants into the ground. ---
examples: Planting ran two weeks late because of the rain.
Everyone works long days during planting.
The soil has to be warm before planting begins.

entries.meaning: The scattering or drilling of seed into prepared ground. ---
examples: Sowing is done by machine on most farms now.
They wait for a dry spell before sowing.
The sowing of winter wheat happens in the fall.
entries.contrast: The verb sow, to plant seed, rhymes with go; the noun sow, a female pig, rhymes with cow.

entries.meaning: The work of pulling unwanted plants out of a field or garden. ---
examples: Weeding the rows by hand took all morning.
She hates weeding more than any other chore.
A thick mulch cuts down on weeding.

entries.meaning: The cutting back of branches so a tree or vine grows better fruit. ---
examples: Pruning is done in late winter, before the buds swell.
Careful pruning keeps the apple trees low enough to pick.
He hired a crew for the pruning this year.

entries.meaning: The separating of grain from the stalks and husks after harvest. ---
examples: Threshing used to bring the whole neighborhood together.
The combine does the cutting and the threshing at once.
Dust hangs in the air all through threshing.

entries.meaning: The feeding of livestock on growing grass, or the land used for it. ---
examples: There's good grazing on the north side of the hill.
Grazing is rotated between four pastures.
The permit allows grazing from May to October.

entries.meaning: The taking of milk from cows, goats, or sheep. ---
examples: Milking starts at four thirty every morning.
The machines cut the milking time in half.
He was late for the evening milking.

entries.meaning: The joining of a shoot from one plant onto the stem of another so they grow as one. ---
examples: Nearly every apple tree you buy is the result of grafting.
Grafting takes a steady hand and a sharp knife.
He learned grafting from his father.

entries.meaning: The preparing and working of land in order to grow crops. ---
examples: Much of this valley is under cultivation.
Cultivation of rice needs a steady water supply.
The field went out of cultivation twenty years ago.

entries.meaning: The process of a seed beginning to grow. ---
examples: Cold soil slows germination.
The seed packet lists a germination rate of ninety percent.
Even moisture is the key to good germination.

entries.meaning: The care and breeding of farm animals, or the careful management of a farm. ---
examples: Good animal husbandry keeps the herd healthy.
He teaches husbandry at the community college.
Careful husbandry got them through a bad year.
entries.contrast: Despite the spelling, it has nothing to do with a husband in the modern sense; it means management of animals and land.

entries.meaning: The growing of fruit, vegetables, and ornamental plants. ---
examples: She has a degree in horticulture.
Horticulture is a bigger business here than grain.
The greenhouse is used for teaching horticulture.

entries.meaning: The science of soil management and crop production. ---
examples: Agronomy covers everything from seed to soil chemistry.
He took a job doing agronomy for a seed company.
The department of agronomy runs test plots each summer.
entries.contrast: Stressed on the second syllable: uh-GRAH-nuh-mee, not AG-ruh-nuh-mee.

entries.meaning: A scientist who advises farmers on soil and crops. ---
examples: The co-op sent an agronomist out to walk the fields.
Two agronomists took soil samples all afternoon.
Ask an agronomist before you change the fertilizer mix.

entries.meaning: The farming of fish, shellfish, or water plants. ---
examples: Most of the catfish sold here comes from aquaculture.
Aquaculture now supplies half the world's seafood.
They moved from row crops into aquaculture.

entries.meaning: The keeping of bees for honey and for pollinating crops. ---
examples: Beekeeping turned into a real side business for them.
He got into beekeeping after he retired.
The class covers beekeeping from hive to harvest.

entries.meaning: The growing of a single crop on the same land year after year. ---
examples: A corn monoculture invites disease.
Monocultures are easy to manage but hard on the soil.
They broke up the monoculture by adding hay to the rotation.

entries.meaning: The keeping of too many animals on land, so the grass cannot recover. ---
examples: Overgrazing left the hillside bare.
Fencing off the creek stopped the overgrazing there.
Years of overgrazing turned good pasture into weeds.

entries.meaning: A grain grown for animal feed and for human food such as oatmeal. ---
examples: He feeds the horses oats twice a day.
The oats are ripe about a month before the corn.
They planted oats as a cover crop.
entries.contrast: Always plural in form — never an oat — and it takes a plural verb: The oats are ripe.

entries.meaning: A tall grain crop grown for animal feed and syrup, common in dry regions. ---
examples: Sorghum handles drought better than corn does.
They switched half the acreage to sorghum.
She poured sorghum syrup over the biscuits.
entries.contrast: The gh is a plain hard g: SOR-guhm.

entries.meaning: A small-seeded grain grown for food and for birdseed. ---
examples: Millet grows well on poor, dry soil.
The birdseed is mostly millet and sunflower.
They plant millet late, after the wheat comes off.

entries.meaning: A deep-rooted plant grown for hay and for feeding cattle. ---
examples: They cut the alfalfa three times a season.
Alfalfa puts nitrogen back into the soil.
The dairy buys alfalfa from a neighbor.

entries.meaning: A crop with bright yellow flowers, grown for its cooking oil. ---
examples: Fields of canola turn the whole valley yellow in June.
Canola has taken over a lot of former wheat ground.
He hauled the canola to the elevator in town.

entries.meaning: A plant of the pea and bean family, whose roots add nitrogen to the soil. ---
examples: Clover and alfalfa are both legumes.
Adding a legume to the rotation cuts fertilizer costs.
Legumes fix nitrogen straight out of the air.
entries.contrast: Americans usually say LEG-yoom, stressing the first syllable.

entries.meaning: Green crops packed tight and left to ferment, used as winter feed for cattle. ---
examples: The cows get silage all through the winter.
They chopped the corn for silage in September.
Good silage smells sweet, not sour.
entries.contrast: The first syllable rhymes with sigh: SY-lij, not SIL-ij.

entries.meaning: Dried food such as hay or straw given to farm animals. ---
examples: There's barely enough fodder to last till spring.
The barn is stacked with fodder.
Corn stalks make rough but usable fodder.

entries.meaning: Grass and other plants that grazing animals eat in the field. ---
examples: There's plenty of forage on the north pasture.
Dry weather left little forage for the herd.
Clover makes excellent forage for sheep.

entries.meaning: The dry outer covering of an ear of corn or a seed. ---
examples: She peeled back the husk to check the kernels.
Husks piled up on the porch steps.
Leave the husk on if you're grilling the corn.

entries.meaning: The hard central part of an ear of corn, which the kernels grow on. ---
examples: We ate corn on the cob with butter and salt.
The pigs got the leftover cobs.
He stripped the kernels off the cob with a knife.

entries.meaning: The light, dry husks separated from grain during threshing. ---
examples: The wind carried the chaff away from the pile.
Chaff got down the back of his shirt.
The combine blows the chaff out the back.

entries.meaning: An upright post driven into the ground to hold up a fence. ---
examples: He set a new fence post every eight feet.
Frost heaved half the fence posts out of the ground.
The wire is stapled to each fence post.

entries.meaning: A thick underground part of a stem, such as a potato, that stores food for the plant. ---
examples: Each plant produced a dozen good-sized tubers.
Store the tubers somewhere cool and dark.
Frost turns a tuber soft and useless.
entries.contrast: Americans say TOO-bur; the British say TYOO-bur.

entries.meaning: A new stem or branch growing from a plant. ---
examples: Green shoots came up a week after the rain.
He pinched off the weak shoot near the base.
The vine sends out a new shoot every few days.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like chute, a sloping channel — same sound, different word.

entries.meaning: Soil worked fine and smooth so that seed can be sown in it. ---
examples: He worked the ground twice to get a fine seedbed.
A rough seedbed gives uneven emergence.
The seedbeds were ready by the first week of April.

entries.meaning: A crop planted to protect and enrich the soil rather than to be sold. ---
examples: He drills a cover crop right after harvest.
Cover crops hold the soil through the winter.
Rye makes a cheap, tough cover crop.

entries.meaning: A crop grown to be sold for money rather than eaten on the farm. ---
examples: Cotton was the main cash crop in this county.
They needed a second cash crop to pay the loan.
Prices for both cash crops fell that fall.

entries.meaning: A machine that presses hay or straw into tight bundles and ties them. ---
examples: The baler jammed halfway down the row.
He bought a used baler at an auction.
Round balers have mostly replaced the square kind.

entries.meaning: A machine that cuts grass or hay. ---
examples: The mower laid the hay down in neat rows.
Both mowers need new blades.
He hitched the mower to the little tractor.

entries.meaning: A machine that beats grain loose from the stalks. ---
examples: An old steam-powered thresher sits in the museum yard.
Threshers used to move from farm to farm each fall.
The thresher roared all afternoon.

entries.meaning: A frame of metal teeth or discs dragged over plowed ground to break up clods. ---
examples: He ran the harrow over the field twice.
The harrow is parked at the end of the lane.
Old wooden harrows hang on the barn wall.

entries.meaning: An implement pulled between crop rows to loosen soil and kill weeds. ---
examples: He ran the cultivator through the beans one more time.
The cultivator shanks need sharpening.
Row-crop cultivators went out of style, then came back.

entries.meaning: A small machine with turning blades that breaks up garden or field soil. ---
examples: He borrowed a tiller to work up the garden.
The tiller wouldn't start after sitting all winter.
Rear-tine tillers handle heavy clay better.

entries.meaning: A machine that spreads liquid chemicals over a crop. ---
examples: The sprayer has booms sixty feet wide.
Rinse the sprayer before you switch chemicals.
Two sprayers covered the whole farm in a day.

entries.meaning: A machine that scatters fertilizer, lime, or manure over a field. ---
examples: He filled the spreader with lime.
The manure spreader threw a fine mist behind it.
Both spreaders were out working the same field.

entries.meaning: A long screw inside a tube, used to move grain or to bore holes for posts. ---
examples: The auger moves corn from the wagon into the bin.
He used a post-hole auger on the fence line.
Keep your hands clear of the auger while it's running.
entries.contrast: Sounds the same as augur, to foretell — a different word entirely.

entries.meaning: A tool or piece of equipment pulled behind a tractor to work the land. ---
examples: Every implement on the place needs greasing.
The dealer sells tractors and implements.
He backed the tractor up to hook onto the implement.
entries.contrast: The noun ends in a weak -muhnt; the verb to implement usually ends in a full -MENT.

entries.meaning: A small plane that sprays chemicals over fields from the air. ---
examples: A crop duster came in low over the cotton.
Crop dusters fly at first light, before the wind picks up.
The crop duster pilot circled and made another pass.

entries.meaning: A tall building where grain is stored and loaded onto trucks or trains. ---
examples: The grain elevator is the tallest thing in town.
Trucks lined up at the grain elevator all morning.
Two grain elevators sit right beside the tracks.

entries.meaning: A round metal container on a farm for storing harvested grain. ---
examples: He put up two more grain bins last year.
Never climb into a grain bin alone.
The grain bin holds about ten thousand bushels.

entries.meaning: A long-handled fork with a few long tines, used for lifting hay or straw. ---
examples: He tossed the hay up with a pitchfork.
Two pitchforks leaned against the barn door.
The handle of the pitchfork was worn smooth.

entries.meaning: A tool with a long curved blade and a bent handle, swung to cut grass or grain by hand. ---
examples: He cut the ditch bank with a scythe.
An old scythe hangs above the workbench.
Scythes have to be sharpened every few minutes.
entries.contrast: The c is silent, and the word rhymes with writhe: SYTHE.

entries.meaning: A short curved blade with a handle, used with one hand for cutting grass or grain. ---
examples: She cut a bundle of herbs with a sickle.
The mower's sickle bar needs new sections.
Sickles were standard tools before machines came along.

entries.meaning: A large heavy knife used for cutting cane, brush, or thick stalks. ---
examples: The workers cut the cane with machetes.
He cleared the path with a machete.
Keep the machete in its sheath when you're not using it.
entries.contrast: The ch is said like sh: muh-SHET-ee.

entries.meaning: A small building where chickens are kept and lay their eggs. ---
examples: She collects the eggs from the henhouse each morning.
A fox got into the henhouse last night.
Both henhouses need fresh straw.

entries.meaning: The upper floor of a barn where hay is stored. ---
examples: The kids hid in the hayloft all afternoon.
He pitched bales down from the hayloft.
Swallows nest in the rafters of the hayloft.

entries.meaning: A building where threshed grain is stored. ---
examples: Mice had gotten into the granary.
The old wooden granary still stands behind the barn.
They emptied both granaries before the sale.

entries.meaning: A pen where pigs are kept. ---
examples: He forked clean straw into the sty.
The pigs came running to the front of the sty.
Both sties were rebuilt with concrete floors.
entries.contrast: Sounds the same as stye, the swollen spot on an eyelid; the plural is sties.

entries.meaning: A fenced enclosure where pigs are raised. ---
examples: The pigpen sits well away from the house.
He hosed out the pigpen every other day.
Your room looks like a pigpen.

entries.meaning: A separate space inside a barn for one animal. ---
examples: Each cow has her own stall.
He mucked out the stalls before breakfast.
The mare kicked the side of her stall all night.

entries.meaning: A place where milk is processed into butter, cream, or cheese. ---
examples: The milk goes to a creamery twenty miles away.
Small creameries have almost all closed.
They sell ice cream at the creamery on weekends.

entries.meaning: A building where farm animals are killed for meat. ---
examples: The cattle are trucked to a slaughterhouse upstate.
Two slaughterhouses serve the whole region.
He worked at a slaughterhouse one summer.
entries.contrast: The -augh- is said like aw and the gh is silent: SLAW-tur-howss.

entries.meaning: A place where beehives are kept. ---
examples: He keeps forty hives at a small apiary by the orchard.
The apiary sits at the edge of the clover field.
Both apiaries produce more than they can sell.

entries.meaning: The room on a dairy farm where cows are milked by machine. ---
examples: Twenty cows fit in the milking parlor at once.
The milking parlor is hosed down twice a day.
They built a new milking parlor last spring.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it parlor; the British spell it parlour.

entries.meaning: An underground room where potatoes, carrots, and other vegetables are kept cool. ---
examples: The potatoes keep all winter in the root cellar.
There's a root cellar dug into the hillside.
Old farmhouses out here all had root cellars.

entries.meaning: A large pile of hay built and left standing in a field. ---
examples: The dog was asleep behind the haystack.
Three haystacks stood at the far end of the meadow.
Finding it was like looking for a needle in a haystack.

entries.meaning: A smaller building standing apart from the main house on a farm. ---
examples: The property includes a barn and three outbuildings.
One outbuilding is used just for tools.
Storms took the roof off the nearest outbuilding.

entries.meaning: A heated glass building for growing plants out of season. ---
examples: The tomatoes came out of a hothouse in February.
They heat the hothouse with a wood stove.
Hothouse flowers cost more in the winter.

entries.meaning: A long narrow channel dug to carry water away from or onto a field. ---
examples: The irrigation ditch runs the length of the field.
They cleaned out the ditches before the spring rain.
His truck slid off the road into the ditch.

entries.meaning: A long narrow groove cut in the soil by a plow. ---
examples: Water ran down every furrow.
He drove a straight furrow the whole length of the field.
The seed drops into the furrow and gets covered over.

entries.meaning: The removal of extra water from soil, or the system that does it. ---
examples: That corner of the field has terrible drainage.
Tile drainage made the low ground farmable.
Good drainage matters more than fertilizer here.

entries.meaning: A pipe or tunnel that carries water under a road or a field lane. ---
examples: The culvert under the driveway is plugged with leaves.
They replaced two rusted culverts last fall.
Water backed up because the culvert was too small.

entries.meaning: A grid of metal bars set into a road that vehicles can cross but cattle will not. ---
examples: The truck rattled over the cattle guard.
There's a cattle guard where the lane leaves the highway.
Two cattle guards keep the herd off the county road.
entries.contrast: Americans call it a cattle guard; the British call the same thing a cattle grid.

entries.meaning: The level below the ground at which the soil is saturated with water. ---
examples: Irrigation has dropped the water table by thirty feet.
The water table is high in the bottomland.
Wells go dry when the water table falls.

entries.meaning: A young female cow that has not yet had a calf. ---
examples: He kept the best heifers for the milking herd.
That heifer will calve in the spring.
They sold twenty heifers at the auction.
entries.contrast: Spelled with ei but pronounced HEF-ur, rhyming with deafer — never HAY-fur.

entries.meaning: A young male cow raised for beef. ---
examples: The steers go to the feedlot in the fall.
He showed a steer at the county fair.
Each steer gains a couple of pounds a day.

entries.meaning: A full-grown pig raised for meat. ---
examples: They raise a couple hundred hogs a year.
The hog weighed nearly three hundred pounds.
Hog prices were down again this month.

entries.meaning: A young female horse. ---
examples: The bay filly was born in April.
Two fillies were turned out in the paddock.
He trained the filly himself.

entries.meaning: A particular type of farm animal, developed by selective mating. ---
examples: That breed of cattle handles cold weather well.
He raises three breeds of chickens.
The dairy breed gives more milk but less beef.

entries.meaning: Someone who raises animals in order to produce young of a particular kind. ---
examples: They bought the bull from a breeder upstate.
Local breeders meet once a year.
A good breeder keeps careful records.

entries.meaning: The bag-shaped organ on a cow, goat, or sheep that produces milk. ---
examples: He wiped the cow's udder before milking.
The udder was swollen and sore.
Udders have to be kept clean to prevent infection.
entries.contrast: In American speech it sounds almost exactly like utter, because the tt is said as a soft d.

entries.meaning: One of the small projections on an animal's udder that the milk comes out of. ---
examples: The calf found the teat on its own.
He attached the machine to all four teats.
One teat was cracked and needed ointment.

entries.meaning: Food that a cow brings back up from its stomach and chews again. ---
examples: The cows lay in the shade chewing their cud.
A calf that won't chew its cud is probably sick.
You can hear them working at the cud in the quiet barn.

entries.meaning: A long open box in a barn that holds hay for horses or cattle. ---
examples: He filled the manger with fresh hay.
The horses pushed their heads into the manger.
Both mangers were built from rough planks.
entries.contrast: The g is soft and the word rhymes with danger: MAYN-jur — not manager.

entries.meaning: A set of straps put on a horse's or cow's head so it can be led. ---
examples: She slipped a halter over the mare's nose.
The halters hang on nails by the stall doors.
He led the calf by a rope halter.

entries.meaning: The straps and fittings that connect a work animal to a plow or wagon. ---
examples: He oiled the leather harness every fall.
The old harnesses still hang in the tack room.
It takes ten minutes to put the harness on a team.

entries.meaning: A rope with a sliding loop, thrown to catch cattle or horses. ---
examples: He swung the lasso over his head twice.
The rider caught the calf with a single lasso throw.
Coiled lassos hung from every saddle.
entries.contrast: Americans usually stress the first syllable, LAS-oh; the British often say luh-SOO.

entries.meaning: A block of salt put out for livestock or deer to lick. ---
examples: He set a salt lick out in the far pasture.
The cattle wore the salt lick down to a nub.
Two salt licks sit near the water trough.

entries.meaning: A numbered plastic tag fastened in a farm animal's ear for identification. ---
examples: Every calf gets an ear tag within a day of birth.
He read the number off the ear tag.
Yellow ear tags mark the animals born this spring.

entries.meaning: The moving of a herd of cattle over a long distance on foot. ---
examples: The cattle drive took three weeks.
Old cattle drives followed the river north.
They still do a short cattle drive every June.

entries.meaning: A dog trained to herd and guard sheep. ---
examples: The sheepdog brought the whole flock in by itself.
Two sheepdogs worked the far side of the hill.
A good sheepdog is worth three farmhands.

entries.meaning: A bell hung on a cow's neck so she can be found in the pasture. ---
examples: You could hear a cowbell somewhere up the hill.
The cowbells clanked as the herd came down.
He hung a cowbell on the lead cow.

entries.meaning: Someone who owns or runs a ranch. ---
examples: The rancher rode out to check the fence.
Local ranchers met about the water rights.
Her father was a cattle rancher all his life.

entries.meaning: Someone paid to do work on a farm. ---
examples: They hired two farmhands for the harvest.
The farmhand was up before dawn.
Good farmhands are hard to find these days.

entries.meaning: A worker paid to help on a farm or ranch, often seasonally. ---
examples: The hired hand slept in a room off the kitchen.
They kept two hired hands through the summer.
He started out as a hired hand and bought the place later.

entries.meaning: A farmer who raises a particular crop to sell. ---
examples: The apple growers had a rough spring.
She buys straight from a local grower.
Every grower in the valley signed the petition.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to take care of sheep. ---
examples: The shepherd moved the flock to higher ground.
Two shepherds stayed with the sheep all night.
He worked as a shepherd in the mountains.
entries.contrast: The middle h is silent: SHEP-urd, not SHEP-hurd.

entries.meaning: Someone who looks after a herd of cattle or other livestock. ---
examples: The herdsman knew every cow by sight.
Two herdsmen brought the cattle down at dusk.
They advertised for an experienced dairy herdsman.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: herdsmen, and the second syllable is weak in both — HURDZ-muhn, HURDZ-muhn.

entries.meaning: A man who herds and tends cattle on horseback. ---
examples: Three cowboys pushed the herd toward the gate.
The cowboy tightened his saddle and swung up.
He worked as a cowboy for two seasons.

entries.meaning: A farmer who works another person's land and pays with part of the crop. ---
examples: His grandparents were sharecroppers in the delta.
The sharecropper never got out from under the debt.
Whole families of sharecroppers moved north for work.

entries.meaning: A doctor who treats animals. ---
examples: The veterinarian came out at midnight for the calving.
Large-animal veterinarians are scarce in rural counties.
She trained as a veterinarian after college.

entries.meaning: An everyday short word for a veterinarian. ---
examples: Call the vet — that cow isn't getting up.
The vet checked the whole herd on Tuesday.
Two vets share the practice in town.
entries.contrast: In other contexts vet is also short for veteran, a former soldier; only the setting tells you which.

entries.meaning: A plant disease that makes leaves and stems wither and die. ---
examples: Blight wiped out the whole potato patch.
Wet weather brings on blight in the tomatoes.
They sprayed early to hold off the blight.
entries.contrast: The gh is silent; it rhymes with light.

entries.meaning: A whitish fungus that grows on damp plants or stored grain. ---
examples: Mildew showed up on the squash leaves in August.
Damp hay in the loft turned to mildew.
A fungicide keeps the mildew off the vines.

entries.meaning: The part of the year warm enough for crops to grow. ---
examples: The growing season here runs from May to September.
A short growing season rules out some crops.
Warm springs have stretched recent growing seasons.

entries.meaning: Wire with sharp points twisted into it, strung to fence in livestock. ---
examples: Three strands of barbed wire run along the property line.
He tore his sleeve on the barbed wire.
Barbed wire changed how the West was fenced.
entries.contrast: Barbed is one syllable — BARBD — even though it is spelled with -ed.

entries.meaning: Light wire mesh with hexagonal holes, used to fence in poultry. ---
examples: He stapled chicken wire around the coop.
A roll of chicken wire leaned against the shed.
Chicken wire keeps the rabbits out of the garden.

entries.meaning: A line of bushes and small trees growing along the edge of a field. ---
examples: Birds nest in the hedgerow between the two fields.
They tore out the hedgerows to make bigger fields.
A thick hedgerow runs the length of the lane.

entries.meaning: A row of trees planted to shelter fields or buildings from the wind. ---
examples: His grandfather planted the windbreak north of the house.
Windbreaks cut down on soil blowing off the field.
Snow drifts up along the windbreak every winter.

entries.meaning: The top layer of soil held together by grass roots. ---
examples: Settlers built houses out of sod.
He cut the sod off before digging the trench.
New sod was laid around the farmhouse.

entries.meaning: Farming carried on as a large-scale commercial industry. ---
examples: Agribusiness has squeezed out a lot of small farms.
He works on the finance side of agribusiness.
The conference was all about agribusiness and trade.

entries.meaning: An outdoor market where farmers sell their produce directly to shoppers. ---
examples: The farmers market opens at seven on Saturdays.
She sells honey at two farmers markets.
We got the peaches at the farmers market.
entries.contrast: Written farmers market, farmers' market, or farmer's market — all three spellings are common in the United States.

entries.meaning: A business owned jointly by farmers, who buy supplies and sell crops through it. ---
examples: He hauls his grain to the co-op in town.
The co-op sells seed, fuel, and fertilizer.
Several small co-ops merged last year.
entries.contrast: Two syllables, KOH-ahp, short for cooperative — not the one-syllable coop, KOOP, where chickens live.

entries.meaning: A farm that keeps cows for their milk.
examples: She grew up on a dairy farm.
Small dairy farms are disappearing fast.
The dairy farm ships milk twice a day.
entries.contrast: Dairy, DAIR-ee, is easy to misread as diary, DY-uh-ree, the book you write in.
